newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin stirs Socialist dreams of regaining power.
newsitem.headline: Jospin stirs Socialist dreams of regaining power.

text.p: Lionel Jospin's combative election campaign has led his opposition Socialist party to dream of a return to power in France. But that may be all, until 2002.

Criss-crossing the country in the month-long campaign, the earnest former education minister has revived the battered party as the uncontested main opposition force four years after it was decimated in a rightwing landslide.

Saying France is in a rut, Jospin, 59, has hammered away at Prime Minister Alain Juppe's government for record unemployment and political sleaze, and accused him of secretly preparing a new austerity to qualify for a single European currency from 1999.

But the school-teacher's son has not managed to convert deep disaffection with the centre-right into a groundswell of support for the Socialist programme, which features pledges to create 700,000 jobs and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss of pay.

Opinion polls have unanimously predicted the centre-right will cling to power in the May 25-June 1 vote. The same surveys show, however, that voters would prefer Jospin as prime minister to the lacklustre Juppe.

But the silver-haired, bespectacled Jospin needs to shake off the tag of "decent loser" he won in 1995 when he gained a better-than-expected 47.3 percent of the vote in a runoff for the presidency won by conservative Jacques Chirac.
Two years ago, it was a compliment. In 1997, it may be an epitaph.

The centre-right says the one-time economics lecturer's pledges of no overall tax hikes do not add up. They portray Jospin as a hostage of the Communist party, an uneasy ally, and accuse him of backtracking in his former enthusiasm for a single currency by setting conditions for joining.

Despite a keen sense of humour, Jospin's speeches often sound as dry and convoluted as university lectures. He has tried to inject more memorable "sound bites" to appeal to the short attention span of television audiences.

The popular television puppet satire "Guignols de L'Info" portrayed him as "Yoyo", a well-meaning simpleton modelled on Enid Blyton's classic "Noddy" aimlessly driving round in a toytown car searching for ideas.

Tall and intense, Jospin had a strict Protestant upbringing in an overwhelmingly Roman Catholic country. Like both Chirac and Juppe, he attended the elite National Administrative College (ENA) -- widely criticised for producing technocratic clones.

If he wins, a prime minister Jospin could make Chirac the longest-lived political lame duck in French history. Chirac called the vote 10 months early, hoping his allies would win and rule in tandem with him until the end of his term in 2002.

But some commentators wonder if Jospin's Socialists are ready for power -- polls show many people do not yet trust them. "Is Jospin scared of winning?" the Evenement du Jeudi weekly magazine asked in a front-page cover.

Even if the Socialists lose, Jospin may be able to bask in the glory of a bigger minority in the 577-member National Assembly in the short term. Polls show the Socialists could easily quadruple the 56 seats they held before the dissolution.

"In the medium term, I don't think Jospin can stay on as party leader after a failure," said sociologist Alain Touraine, predicting the Socialists would have to reform towards the centre like British Prime Minister Tony Blair's Labour party.
And that would probably mean a younger generation at the top, he said.

Jospin is irritated by suggestions his Socialists are a more archaic version of the left than Britain's Labour, which ended 18 years of Conservative rule this month, or that they are beguiled by an outmoded belief in strong state control.
"The old idea that the right knows how to manage and that the left only knows how to spend is well and truly out of date," Jospin wrote during the campaign.
Asked by one interviewer what separates him from Blair, he retorted: "The Channel. But with the tunnel..."
